records.title: Choosing, sharpening and cleaning pruning tools for a bush rose

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The thickness at which hand pruners give way to loppers differs between sources: three-quarters of an inch in two rose sources, half an inch in a general woody-plant text (C8). Sources name bypass pruners without giving a reason, and one recommends anvil pruners for dead wood (C9). Sources differ on what to disinfect with and how often, and none cites evidence of effectiveness (C10). No source compares sharp and blunt tools directly; the advice rests on practitioner agreement (AF-27).

content.heading: Your tools

items.text: Match the tool to the stem: bypass hand pruners for thin canes, loppers for thicker ones, and a pruning saw for the thickest or oldest canes.
Hand pruners are for stems up to about three-quarters of an inch (about 2 cm) thick. Use loppers or a saw above that.
Use bypass (scissor-action) pruners. Anvil pruners are fine for clearing dead wood only.
Keep your tools sharp and clean, so each cut is clean and doesn't crush the cane.
Wipe the blades with 70 percent alcohol between plants, and after cutting out diseased wood. A sensible precaution, not a strict rule.

records.title: Making a pruning cut on a bush rose: removing a whole stem, or shortening one back to a bud

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Distance above the bud (C2): most sources say about a quarter inch; a few say up to half an inch. Both are defensible answers to the same tradeoff (too close risks killing the bud; too far risks the stub dying back). All the quarter-inch sources are from the United States. Slant direction (C3): most sources say "away from the bud"; a few say "in the same direction as the bud", and it's unresolved whether that's the same technique. Whether angle and bud direction matter at all (C11): rose societies in South Australia and South Africa say they matter little, or recommend a straight cut; neither gives a reason. The approved default keeps the majority convention. Sealing (C4, AF-30, AF-35): most sources, including every UK and New Zealand source, don't mention it. Where rose sources recommend it, the reason is to keep cane-boring insects out of the soft pith, not to help the cut heal. General tree research finds that wound dressings don't help healing, which answers a different question. No trial of sealed against unsealed rose canes was found. Stubs (AF-29): five of the nine sources are about dead canes, so whether the rule applies equally to every kind of removal isn't directly addressed. Two kinds of cut (AF-31): only one of the three sources is rose-specific. Outward bud (AF-21): two sources allow an exception for a cane that already spreads sideways.

removeStem.text: Cut the stem off where it starts: at the base, at the bud union, or where it joins its parent stem. Don't leave a stub.

shorten.text: Cut just above a bud that faces outward, away from the centre of the bush.
Cut about a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) above the bud. Up to half an inch is also fine if you'd rather avoid the stub dying back.
Make the cut on a slant, at roughly 45 degrees, not flat.
Slant the cut away from the bud.

seal.text: On cuts roughly pencil-thick or larger, you can seal the end with wood glue, nail polish or pruning sealer, to keep cane-boring insects out. Thinner cuts don't need it.

records.title: Advisory: removing no more than about a third of a bush in one session (general pruning guidance, not rose-specific)

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: This is a general rule for shrubs and trees, not tested on roses. One rose-specific source recommends a hard, one-time renovation instead, which suggests the rule is a cautious default rather than a rose requirement (AF-40). The NC State wording is about a plant's crown in any one year, not about a single session (WEAKCONGESTED AF-18). No source links the choice between one hard cutback and a staged approach to a particular bush's condition (AF-40). A fifth source listed for AF-40 (Colorado State University, Adams County) couldn't be confirmed and isn't cited.

content.heading: How much to remove
content.label: General pruning guidance, not specific to roses

items.text: A general pruning rule for shrubs and trees is to remove no more than about a third of a plant's growth in one session. Removing more can stress the plant, drain its stored energy and cause a flush of uncontrolled regrowth.
One general source puts it as no more than a third of a plant's crown in any one year.
If an overgrown bush needs more than that, the same guidance spreads the work over two or three years, about a third at a time.
This rule hasn't been tested on roses, and at least one rose source recommends a single hard renovation instead. Treat it as a cautious guide, not a limit.

content.label: General pruning guidance, with what rose growers do

records.title: Growing-season care for a Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); general care outside pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Feeding and deadheading: when to stop depends on the region, and no single date is given (F4, F5). Mulch depth: sources give 2 to 4 inches (Source Register §3, matter 4). Watching for problems: this record doesn't diagnose anything (F6). The "notice first" framing rests on one source (F12). The claim that growing conditions cause most decline is also single-source (F13). Region: all sources are UK or US (ARC §5).

content.heading: Growing-season care

items.text: Water deeply and less often, rather than a little and often. In the growing season, aim for roughly 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) of water a week, counting rain, when it's dry.
Spread organic mulch about 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) deep around the base — bark, well-rotted manure, wood chips or pine needles — kept a few inches clear of the stems.
Start feeding in spring as new growth begins, feed again through summer, and stop by mid-to-late summer so new growth can toughen before winter. Stop earlier where winter comes earlier.
Remove faded flowers through the growing season to encourage more. Stop in early-to-mid autumn, so the rose can form hips and slow down for winter.
Watch for blackspot, powdery mildew, aphids and spider mites. Water at the base, or in the morning if you water from above, to keep the leaves drier.
Look over the leaves, buds and stems regularly for yellowing, spots, dropping leaves, stunted or twisted growth, or fewer flowers. Noticing early is the useful first step.
If your rose looks unwell, think about its growing conditions first: uneven watering, soggy soil or extreme weather. One extension service says these cause most decline.

content.disclosure: This care advice comes mainly from UK and US gardening services. Timings and amounts may differ where you live.

records.title: Caring for a recently planted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose that PKR-SGT-000002 has stopped (planted less than about three years ago, or establishment not shown)
common.preserved_uncertainty: F7 concerns roughly the first year. F2's closer watering covers roughly the first two years. The pruning wait (PKR-SGT-000002) is about three years or more. These are three different questions and are stated separately, not merged (ARC F2 limitations). The gate's own question is about three years, so item 1 is worded for the gardener to apply if the rose went in within about the past year.

content.heading: Caring for a recently planted rose

items.text: If your rose was planted within about the past year, leave as much of its leaves and stems as you can this first season. Only remove faded flowers, and don't cut stems for the vase. A new rose uses its leaves to make the energy it needs to grow roots.
Pay closer attention to watering for roughly the first two years after planting.
Full pruning usually waits until a rose has been in the ground about three years. I'll check this again next time.

records.title: Preparing a Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose for winter

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003), in an area with hard winter frosts
common.preserved_uncertainty: Winter mounding applies where winters bring hard frosts (F9). Mound heights vary between sources, from 8 to 18 inches, around the common 10–12 (Source Register §3, matter 4). Collars and wraps rest on two sources and are described particularly for climbing roses or exposed sites (F10). All sources are from the US (ARC §5).

content.heading: Preparing for winter
content.label: If your winters bring hard frosts…

items.text: Once the rose has had several hard frosts and gone dormant, mound soil, compost or mulch about 10–12 inches (25–30 cm) high around the base, covering the graft union. Remove the mound in spring once hard frosts have passed.
For colder or exposed spots, sources also describe a collar of tar paper or wire mesh filled with straw, pine bark or peat moss, or wrapping canes in burlap or evergreen boughs.
Water thoroughly after the first hard frost and before the ground freezes, and clear fallen leaves from around the plant before winter.

records.title: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The view that pruning does not kill a rose is expert opinion, not measured (AF-1). One commercial website disagrees, saying cutting back too far "could stress it out or even kill it" (AF-20, Very Low; C-1). Sources disagree on whether "weak" means the whole plant or a single shoot (C-2), and on renovating in one go or in stages (C-4). Newly planted roses are outside this record.

content.heading: Can pruning too hard kill or harm my rose?

items.text: Rose societies, rose growers and a botanic garden in New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US say pruning, even hard or badly done, doesn't kill an established rose.
Some of them add conditions: the rose is otherwise healthy, it isn't cut below the ground line, and its roots are intact.
The cut sources say can lose a rose is one made below the graft or below the ground line.
A weak or slow-growing rose is pruned less hard than a vigorous one. Within a bush, sources still cut single weak shoots back further or remove them.
Pruning before the frosts have passed risks frost damage to the new growth and dieback.
Sources describe any harm from pruning too hard as a short-term setback. One says the first year after a hard pruning is a recovery year.
An old or neglected rose can be brought back with hard pruning.
Pip's approach to a heavy renovation is to spread it over two or three years, about a third at a time. Some sources do it all in one go, and none gives a rule for choosing.
Sources give no signs or waiting time for judging recovery. If no new growth appears during the growing season, ask your local rose society.

records.title: Why isn't my rose flowering?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source gives a tested way to tell the causes apart, or says which is most common (R-1). Sources disagree on sun hours (C-1), on feeding (C-2), on where to cut a blind shoot (C-4), on first-season flowering (C-5), on how hard is too hard (C-6) and on chemical treatment of balling (C-7). Rose midge has no New Zealand or Australian source (R-3). Lower-confidence findings (potassium AF-7, heat AF-9, cold AF-10, hips AF-20, rootstock AF-32, pesticides AF-33) are not used in this answer.

content.heading: Why isn't my rose flowering?

items.text: Pip can't tell you which reason applies to your rose. Here are the reasons sources give, with what to look for and what they suggest.
Too little sun, or too much shade, means fewer flowers.
Sources give a minimum of four to eight hours of direct sun a day. Six is the most common figure.
Trees and shrubs nearby compete with a rose for light, water and food. Sources advise planting roses away from them.
Too much fertiliser, especially nitrogen, gives lots of leafy growth and few flowers.
Too little feeding is also given as a reason, and feeding as a remedy. Pip's care tips give the feeding pattern.
Too little water, or drought, reduces flowering. Sources describe pale, limp leaves, dropped leaves and small flowers.
Pruning too much, too little or at the wrong time is listed as a reason. No source says where too much begins.
Harder pruning gives fewer, larger flowers. Lighter pruning gives more, smaller ones.
Removing spent flowers from a repeat-flowering rose encourages more flowers.

If your rose flowered once in late spring or early summer and not again, it may be a once-flowering variety. Pip can't support those yet. A local rose society or garden centre can help, or you can check its type with Pip's rose-type questions.
Pruning a once-flowering rose before it flowers removes its flowers.
A blind shoot grows and leafs normally but has no flower bud at its tip.
The cause of blind shoots isn't known. Sources suggest weather, shade, over-feeding and big swings between day and night temperatures.
Sources cut a blind shoot back to get a new shoot that can flower. The RHS cuts it back by half to a strong bud. Others cut to the next leaf joint down, or to the next full five-leaflet leaf.
Buds that form but don't open after cool, wet weather may be "balled": the bud feels soft and its outer petals turn brown and papery.
Sources remove balled or rotting buds promptly, and suggest better air flow around the plant and watering at the base, not over the leaves.
Sources link spotted petals with grey fuzz to grey mould (botrytis), which is more common in cool, wet weather.
Sources link brown or white streaks on petals, or distorted flowers, to thrips.
Sources link holes in buds, with caterpillars, to budworm.
Black spot (dark spots on the leaves, then yellowing and leaf drop) weakens a rose so it flowers less.
A photo alone can't show why a rose isn't flowering. Check these signs on the plant itself.

records.title: Should I spray my roses?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources disagree on whether to use fungicides at all (C-1): the Royal Horticultural Society recommends against them, and three sources say spraying is needed or helps. They also differ on how long a variety's resistance lasts (C-3). Three of the New Zealand sources for growing without spraying describe one garden, and the University of California ties its statement to dry climates. No source was found on which disease-tolerant varieties suit New Zealand (R-3).

content.heading: Should I spray my roses?

items.text: Roses can be grown well with little or no spraying, especially if you grow disease-tolerant varieties.
Choose disease-tolerant varieties to reduce disease.
A variety's resistance can differ from region to region. One source says it may not last.
One source says popular Hybrid Teas and Floribundas are often prone to black spot.
Treat pesticides as a last resort, after other measures.

Experts disagree on whether roses need spraying. The better-supported view is that they can be grown well with little or none. Some say disease-prone roses need fungicide, or that regular spraying helps. The Royal Horticultural Society advises against fungicides altogether.
I couldn't find a list of disease-tolerant varieties that suit New Zealand. A local rose society is the place to ask.
If you spray, use only a product labelled for roses where you live, and follow its label.

records.title: What can I do about leaf disease without spraying?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Keeping leaves dry helps against black spot, but sources say water on the leaves can reduce powdery mildew (C-4). The Royal Horticultural Society allows burying fallen leaves under mulch, where other sources bin or burn them. "Most common" for black spot comes from one rose society. No source gives a mechanism or a measure for a well-fed rose resisting disease.

content.heading: What can I do about leaf disease without spraying?

items.text: Black spot is tied to wet leaves.
Clear away fallen leaves and cut out infected stems, especially before and during winter. This reduces disease the next season.
Remove infected leaves and shoots as soon as you see them.
Put diseased leaves and prunings in the rubbish, not the compost.
Avoid watering over the leaves, and keep them dry. One source says to water around the roots.
For powdery mildew, wetting the leaves in mid-morning or the middle of the day, in dry weather, can reduce it.
Give roses sun, space and moving air. These reduce leaf disease.
A rose that is watered and fed well is more likely to resist disease.

records.title: Which sprays are used for black spot and mildew?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The Royal Horticultural Society recommends against all fungicides, organic types included (C-1). Sources disagree about home-made sprays, and neither view is clearly better supported (C-8). The University of California doesn't list copper for black spot, and a gardener writing to the Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture reported disease in wet weather despite a copper spray. Wisconsin says neem oil gives only "some" control. The synthetic fungicides are named by US sources; which spray types are approved for home gardeners in each country was not established (R-1). Brand names and mixing amounts are not given.

content.heading: Which sprays are used for black spot and mildew?

items.text: Oils, including neem oil, and sulphur are used against black spot and powdery mildew. One source also names potassium bicarbonate.
Copper sprays are used against black spot.

US university sources name synthetic fungicides for black spot, most often chlorothalonil. I couldn't find which are approved for home gardeners in each country, so use only a product labelled for roses where you live.
Experts disagree about home-made sprays such as a baking soda mix. Some suggest them. The Royal Horticultural Society advises against them, because they are unregulated and usually untested.
I name types of spray, not brands. For how much to use, follow the product's label.
One source says not to put oil on a plant that is short of water, or within two weeks of a sulphur spray.
If you spray, use only a product labelled for roses where you live, and follow its label.

records.title: If I spray, when and how often?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources disagree on spraying regularly through the season or only when a problem appears, and neither view is clearly better supported (C-2). Stated intervals differ by product and are set by the label (C-7). The season window is stated for regular-spraying programmes only. No New Zealand source compares regions (R-4).

content.heading: If I spray, when and how often?

items.text: Fungicides protect leaves before infection. They generally don't cure it, so timing matters.
Experts disagree on when to spray. Some spray regularly through the growing season to prevent disease. Others spray only when there is a problem.
If you spray regularly, start with the first new leaves after winter and carry on through the growing season, or until wet weather passes.
Repeat intervals range from weekly to about every two weeks. The product label sets the interval.
One source says roses may need spraying more often in a bad outbreak. Another says to consider spraying ahead of disease where a rose has had black spot badly and a wet season is forecast.
Alternate between types of fungicide, so the disease is slower to become resistant to them.
I couldn't find anything that compares how much spraying is needed in different parts of New Zealand. A local rose society is the place to ask.
If you spray, use only a product labelled for roses where you live, and follow its label.

records.title: What about a winter spray after pruning?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: New Zealand and Australian sources describe a winter spray; the UK and US institutional pages consulted don't describe a spray after pruning (C-5). No source tests whether it makes a difference (R-2). Sources differ on the order and timing of the winter sprays (C-6). Most of the sources are commercial, and the New Zealand Rose Society article dates from 1996. What the winter spray is said to achieve (AF-27) and that copper washes off in rain (AF-43) are on record only. Where the spray goes (AF-26) is on record only, at Low, after a correction to the research record.

content.heading: What about a winter spray after pruning?

items.text: Rose sources in New Zealand and Australia describe a clean-up spray in winter, usually after pruning. Their advice ranges from highly recommended to optional.
For the winter clean-up spray, New Zealand and Australian sources name lime sulphur, copper and a spraying oil.
For copper, sources differ on timing: after winter pruning, through winter into early spring, or at the first sign of spring growth.
One source says not to use lime sulphur and copper sprays within two weeks of each other.
One source says never to mix lime sulphur and oil, or spray them together.
I couldn't find a test of whether a winter spray makes a difference. A local rose society is the place to ask what works near you.

The UK and US university and horticultural-society pages I checked don't describe a spray after pruning. Several advise clearing fallen leaves in autumn or winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.
If you spray, use only a product labelled for roses where you live, and follow its label.

records.title: How do I spray safely?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Protective equipment, cleaning the sprayer, heat and the three statements on what not to combine are each given by one or two sources; they are included as precautions. The evening-only timing rests on one consumer-organisation source. No Australian or US regulator page was read, and which spray types are approved for home gardeners in each country was not established (R-1).

content.heading: How do I spray safely?

items.text: Read and follow the product label. In the UK this is a legal requirement.
Which products are allowed differs by country and changes over time. I couldn't find which spray types are approved in each country, so use only a product labelled for roses where you live.
Don't spray open flowers. One source says to spray only in the evening, once bees are back in their hives.
Wear gloves and safety gear, and clean the sprayer afterwards.
One source says never to spray in the heat of the day.
One source says not to use lime sulphur and copper sprays within two weeks of each other.
One source says never to mix lime sulphur and oil, or spray them together.
One source says not to put oil on a plant that is short of water, or within two weeks of a sulphur spray.

records.title: What should I do about aphids?

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Soaps and oils for aphids are stated by two extension services and one nursery. Sprays for other pests (spider mites, scale, thrips, caterpillars, beetles) were outside the commissioned questions and are not covered (R-6).

content.heading: What should I do about aphids?

items.text: Put up with a few aphids, hose them off, and let their natural enemies deal with them. One source also says to squash them by hand.
Insecticidal soaps and horticultural oils can be used on aphids. One source says they have only a moderate effect on aphids' natural enemies.
Broad-spectrum and higher-toxicity insecticides can harm natural enemies, and that can bring pests back.
If you spray, use only a product labelled for roses where you live, and follow its label.

records.title: When can I plant or move a rose?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Planting months differ by country and climate (C-3): the UK source gives late autumn or late winter to early spring, and cold-winter US sources prefer or require spring. New Zealand months come from garden centres only, and May in Australia from one source. Three New Zealand sources speak of roses in general, not bare-root roses. For potted roses two New Zealand pages still give a best season. Sources differ on the best point in the dormant season to move a rose (C-9).

content.heading: When can I plant or move a rose?

items.text: Plant a bare-root rose (one sold without soil on its roots) while it is dormant, with no leaves, between late autumn and early spring. One source says to avoid the middle of winter when the ground is frozen.
In New Zealand, winter is the best time to plant a rose, and roses can be planted on through spring. One garden centre says new-season roses reach the shops from June. Months are only a guide.
In Australia, plant bare-root roses in winter, while they are dormant. Two rose societies say June or July, and one source says from May. Months are only a guide.
In the UK, plant bare-root roses in late autumn, or from late winter to early spring before growth starts.

In the US, where winters are very cold, spring is the preferred time to plant bare-root roses. One source puts the line at winters that fall below -10 °F, and says that where it stays warmer than that, autumn or spring both work.
A rose in a pot can be planted over a longer season than a bare-root rose. UK and New Zealand sources say all year, and two US sources say through the growing season.
items.limit: One source says not to plant into frozen or very dry ground. Another says to keep it well watered if you plant in spring or summer. One New Zealand source says autumn or winter is still the best time.

items.text: Move an established rose while it is dormant, which means it is not actively growing. Most sources say winter. Some say late autumn or early spring.

In New Zealand, one garden centre says the best time to move a rose is after pruning in July, while it is dormant, and once the risk of frost has passed. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
A rose can be moved in the growing season if you have to. It will need extra watering afterwards.

records.title: Where should I plant a rose?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The minimum hours of sun stated range from four to six. For heavy soil, some sources suggest raised beds or mounds and others gypsum, some with compost. Stated spacing differs, and only one figure is said of a bush rose. Why roses are spaced is disputed (C-8), which is on record only.

content.heading: Where should I plant a rose?

items.text: Choose a sunny spot. Sources give a minimum of four to six hours of direct sun a day.
Roses need soil that drains well. Where the soil is heavy or drains poorly, some sources suggest a raised bed or mound, and others suggest digging in gypsum or compost.
Keep roses away from the roots of nearby trees and shrubs, which compete with them.

How far apart to plant depends on the type of rose and how big it will grow, so check the label. Where sources give a distance, it is about 50 cm to 1 m (20 inches to 3 feet). One gives 75 to 90 cm (2½ to 3 feet) for hybrid tea roses.
A new rose planted where a rose grew before may struggle to establish and may grow poorly. One source suggests choosing a spot where roses haven't grown.

records.title: How do I plant a rose?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Soaking times differ from one hour to 24 hours (C-2). Storage advice for a bare-root rose differs. Hole sizes differ. Sources disagree on pruning at planting (C-6), consistent with the conflict preserved in ARC-BUSHROSE-RECENTPLANT-01. One source cuts the whole root system back by a third, and one says not to cut roots that are too large for the hole. The mound method is described mainly by Australian sources. Planting a potted rose at its container depth rests on two New Zealand sources.

content.heading: How do I plant a rose?

items.text: Plant a bare-root rose (one sold without soil on its roots) soon after you get it, and don't let its roots dry out.

If you can't plant a bare-root rose straight away, keep it in its packaging somewhere cool and safe from frost. One source allows up to two weeks, with the roots kept moist, and another up to three weeks.
Soak the roots of a bare-root rose in water before planting.

Soak a bare-root rose's roots for anywhere from one hour to 24 hours before planting. Sources differ within that range. Two say not to soak for longer than 24 hours, and one of them says it may damage the roots.
Trim off any damaged or broken roots before planting. One source says not to cut off roots that are too large for the hole, but to dig a bigger hole.
Dig the planting hole wider than the roots. Several sources say about twice as wide.
For a bare-root rose, make a mound of soil in the bottom of the hole and spread the roots over it.
Plant a potted rose at the same depth it was growing in its pot. Advice on where the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted) should sit differs, so check that too.
Water the rose in well as soon as it is planted.

Experts disagree on whether to prune a bare-root rose at planting. Some cut the stems back when they plant. One source says a packaged rose has already been pruned and rarely needs more, and another prunes in the first winter after planting.

records.title: How deep should I plant the bud union?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Recommended bud-union depth differs: above the soil, at soil level or below it (C-1), consistent with ARC-BUSHROSE-SUCKERS-01 AF-12. The difference follows climate in the sources that give a reason. No New Zealand non-commercial source states a depth, and none addresses New Zealand's colder districts (R-2). In the UK a rose nursery buries the union where the Royal Horticultural Society says not to. No source was read for countries other than New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US.

content.heading: How deep should I plant the bud union?

items.text: Experts disagree on how deep to plant the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted). Advice ranges from up to 5 cm (2 inches) above the soil, to level with it, to as much as 10 cm (4 inches) below. Sources that give a reason for burying it are speaking of places with cold winters, and say it protects the rose from the cold. Two sources give reasons against burying it: a reported risk of dieback, and, in mild climates, disease at the union.
In New Zealand and Australia, plant the bud union level with the soil or up to 5 cm above it.

In the UK, sources differ on the bud union. One says to plant it at soil level, not below, because burying it is reported to raise the risk of dieback. A UK rose nursery sets it about 5 cm below the soil when replanting a rose.

In the US, extension sources in places with cold winters plant the bud union below the soil, from slightly below to 4 inches (about 10 cm) down. In one mild area, one source plants it an inch above. Ask your local extension service what is done where you live.
I couldn't find advice on how deep to plant the bud union in New Zealand's colder districts. A local rose society is the place to ask.
The advice I found on how deep to plant the bud union comes from New Zealand, Australia, the UK and the US. If your rose is somewhere else, a local rose society is the place to ask.

records.title: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources disagree on how real replant disease is and what to do about it (C-4). No comparison of remedies in home gardens was found (R-3). The amount of soil to replace differs, including between two pages of the same body. That the cause is not established (AF-12), and that the problem can persist for at least nine years (AF-14, one source, not said of roses), are not used.

content.heading: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?

items.text: A new rose planted where a rose grew before may struggle to establish and may grow poorly. This is called replant disease.

If you plant in the same spot, swap the soil in the planting hole for fresh soil from another part of the garden. Sources differ on how much to take out: from two buckets of soil, along with the old rose's roots, to a hole 45 to 60 cm (18 to 24 inches) across and 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 inches) deep. One source gives planting somewhere else as another option.

Experts disagree about replant disease. Several advise replacing the soil. One rose specialist calls that the old method and instead adds compost or well-rotted manure and treats the new rose with mycorrhizal fungi. That source reports that opinion is divided on whether the problem is real.
I couldn't find a comparison of which remedy for replant disease works best in a home garden. A local rose society is the place to ask.

records.title: How do I move an established rose?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: How much to cut back before a move differs widely (C-5). Sources differ on whether to keep the soil on the roots (C-10). Stated digging distances mix distance out from the plant with width across. Evidence on moving comes mainly from nurseries, garden companies, rosarians and short extension answers; all New Zealand moving sources are commercial (R-4). No source gives success rates or a rose-specific age limit (R-1). That moving a rose is forgiving (AF-35) is on record only (C-7).

content.heading: How do I move an established rose?

items.text: Move an established rose while it is dormant, which means it is not actively growing. Most sources say winter. Some say late autumn or early spring.

In New Zealand, one garden centre says the best time to move a rose is after pruning in July, while it is dormant, and once the risk of frost has passed. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

Cut the top growth back before a winter move. Sources differ on how much: from cutting it back by a third, to cutting it down to 25 to 30 cm (10 to 12 inches), to cutting it right back to 3 to 5 buds above the base.

Dig wide around the rose and keep as many of the roots as you can. Sources give different distances, from about 25 cm (10 inches) out from the base to as much as 60 cm (24 inches), and one says the larger the better.

Sources differ on the soil around the roots. For a winter move, one shakes the soil off and replants the rose like a bare-root one, and one says to keep as large a root ball as you can. For a move in the growing season, one says to keep as much soil on the roots as possible.
One source says it is very important to keep the roots moist until the rose is replanted. Another waters the soil well the day before the move.
Water the rose well once it is replanted, and keep it watered until it recovers. Sources differ on how long: from every day for a week or two, to watering in dry spells through the first year.
A rose can be moved in the growing season if you have to. It will need extra watering afterwards. Sources disagree on whether to cut it back first.
One source says a rose that has been settled for many years becomes tricky to move. Another lists roses among plants that dislike having their roots disturbed.
I couldn't find how often a moved rose survives, or an age beyond which a rose is too old to move. A local rose society is the place to ask.

records.title: Which months do I prune my rose?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose in New Zealand; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources differ within the June to August window (C-1). One company says cooler places prune earlier, against the rest (C-2). Times for the north differ by up to a month (C-3). Christchurch is placed differently by two sources (C-4). Southern sources differ between late July and August (C-10). Two companies differ on whether to wait for the leaves to fall (C-12). No source draws a boundary for 'up north' or 'colder parts'. Months for the north, Northland, Auckland, Whanganui, Masterton, Canterbury, Christchurch and Dunedin each rest on one organisation or on garden companies. No New Zealand source names bud swell; three say to prune before growth starts.

content.heading: Which months do I prune my rose?

items.text: In New Zealand, the main winter pruning is done between June and August, depending on where you live. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.
Prune later where it is colder: the north starts earlier than the south. One garden company says the opposite: that cooler places can prune earlier, once all the leaves have fallen.
Up north, one source says pruning starts around early July. Another says it can start a little before July. Months are only a guide.
In the colder parts of the South Island, pruning gets under way in August. In Dunedin, one source prunes in late July. Months are only a guide.
In Northland, one garden company says the end of July to early August is a good time to prune. Months are only a guide.
In Auckland, one garden service says to prune in July. One garden company says June to July, before the rose bursts into leaf, which can be as early as August in Auckland. Months are only a guide.
In Whanganui, one garden centre manager says roses are best pruned in July. Months are only a guide.
In Masterton, one garden company says to prune in July to August. Months are only a guide.

In Canterbury, one source says pruning can begin towards the end of July in milder parts and be completed there in August. Colder areas may prefer to wait until August, and colder inland districts prune once the worst frosts have passed. It says to finish winter pruning in September. Months are only a guide.
In Christchurch, one garden company says to leave pruning until late winter or early spring, after the last frost.

In Dunedin, one source prunes its modern roses in late July, when they are most dormant and the worst frosts are over. In a frosty spot that can mean waiting until mid-August. One garden company says June or July, and August if you are unsure. Months are only a guide.
Prune in winter, when the rose is dormant and not in active growth. In colder or frosty places, wait until the worst frosts have passed.
Don't leave pruning too late: prune before the rose bursts into growth.
Don't prune too early, because frost can damage the new growth that follows.

Two garden companies differ on a rose that still has its leaves or flowers in June. One says to wait until it is fully dormant, with no leaves left, which may mean pruning in July. The other says a rose can be pruned even if it is still flowering. Months are only a guide.

provenance.note: Approved by a Founder in chat on 7 October 2026 (Pip's Answers, New Zealand months). Published by KIT.

records.title: When do I start and stop feeding?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose in New Zealand; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Months for the first feed differ from late August to mid-late October (C-6) and come mostly from companies. Sources conflict on the last feed, from the end of February to early April, and two companies feed through autumn (C-5). One company's advice to wait for the last frosts in frosty areas is given as a precaution (AF-20). No non-commercial New Zealand source names a month for the last feed (R-2).

content.heading: When do I start and stop feeding?

items.text: Start feeding in spring, as new growth appears.
In New Zealand, the first feed is usually given in September. It can be as early as late August or as late as mid to late October. Months are only a guide.
In a frosty area, one source says it is better to wait until the last frosts before you feed your roses.

Sources disagree on when to stop feeding. One says no later than the end of February, so that the canes (stems) can harden before winter. Others say March or early April, and some feed through autumn. Months are only a guide.

records.title: When do I stop deadheading?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose in New Zealand; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The times to stop come from two garden companies and one garden service, about a month apart (C-9). Other pages name no time to stop, and one says to deadhead throughout the flowering season. No New Zealand source gives a month to stop summer pruning (AF-25).

content.heading: When do I stop deadheading?

items.text: Deadhead (remove the faded flowers) while the rose is flowering. Two garden companies say when to stop: one at the end of February, and one at the end of March, leaving the last flowers so that hips (the rose's fruit) can form. Months are only a guide.

In Auckland, one garden service says to stop deadheading from March, so that the rose can form hips and rest before winter. Another Auckland source says to keep removing dead flowers all through the flowering season. Months are only a guide.
I couldn't find when to stop summer pruning (a light prune in summer to encourage more flowers) in New Zealand. A local rose society is the place to ask.

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose in New Zealand; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Named planting months come from one company nationally and from one organisation for Canterbury. content.heading: Which months do I plant or move a rose?

items.text: In New Zealand, winter is the best time to plant a rose, and planting can go on through spring. One garden company says June and July are the best months. Months are only a guide.
New roses for winter planting reach garden centres from June. Months are only a guide.

In Canterbury, one source says to plant roses in June, July and August, while they are dormant. July and August are its months for bare-root roses, which are sold without soil on their roots. Months are only a guide.
In Auckland, one source says roses are best planted in autumn or winter.
A rose in a pot can be planted at any time of year. Keep it well watered if you plant in spring or summer.
Move an established rose in winter, while it is dormant. One garden centre page says autumn instead.

For moving a rose, one garden centre says July, after pruning and once the risk of frost has passed. One garden company says June or July. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

records.title: When do I clear up and spray in winter?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose in New Zealand; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources differ on whether a winter spray goes on before or after pruning (C-11). Months for the spray come from a 1996 rose society article, one rose columnist and two garden centres. Sources differ on how long to keep lime sulphur apart from other sprays (AF-47). Follow-up sprays differ from page to page and are on record only (AF-34). No New Zealand source describes covering or mounding roses for winter (AF-35). Whether a winter spray makes a measurable difference is not established (ARC-BUSHROSE-SPRAYING-01).

content.heading: When do I clear up and spray in winter?

items.text: Clear away fallen and diseased leaves in autumn and winter, and pick up the prunings and fallen leaves after pruning. Burn them or put them in the rubbish, not the compost.
In Canterbury, one source says to remove diseased leaves from roses in May, June and July. Months are only a guide.

If you use a clean-up spray in winter (a spray meant to clear pests and diseases left on the plant), put it on at pruning or just after. Some put a first spray on in June, before pruning. Months are only a guide, and the label on the spray comes first.
In New Zealand, lime sulphur, copper and a spraying oil are used as winter sprays. Follow the label on the spray.
One source says lime sulphur strips the leaves from new growth, so if you use it as a winter spray, put it on at pruning time and don't leave it too late. Follow the label on the spray.

If you use lime sulphur, never mix it with other sprays, and leave two to three weeks before you use a copper spray. One garden centre says to wait three weeks before any other spray. Follow the label on the spray.
I couldn't find New Zealand advice on covering roses or mounding soil over the base for winter. A local rose society is the place to ask.

records.title: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?

common.applies_to: Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose in New Zealand; answer to a common question
common.preserved_uncertainty: The frost statements come from one source, the national climate research institute, and are about climate, not roses. That the garden itself matters is one botanic garden's point. No rose source draws a boundary for its climate bands (AF-3). Whether the institute's 'north of Waikato' matches the 'up north' of rose sources is the ROC's own question and is not used (R-5a).

content.heading: How do I allow for frost and my own garden?

items.text: When to prune depends on where you live. Go by your own garden too: one source says the right time can differ even within one suburb, and that a frosty spot can mean waiting longer.

Frosts are common in the cooler months in most of New Zealand, the national climate institute says. They are rare north of Waikato, less frequent near the coast, and most frequent at inland South Island places such as Alexandra. They can still happen anywhere.
Your garden is more likely to get frost if it is on flat ground where cold air can't drain away, or in a valley or basin, the national climate institute says. Frost can vary widely over a small area.
Your local rose society can advise on timing for your own climate.

records.title: Dead vs. living wood — cut/leave decision

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning, or the removal-only session of PKR-SGT-000001 v1.1 §2.1

decision_notes.text: Remove it back into living tissue — white or pale-green pith and green bark — not just to the first sign of dead tissue.
If dieback carries on after repeated cuts, keep going toward the bud union, or remove the whole cane.

records.title: Crossing or rubbing stems — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Only 2 of about 16 sources give any rule for which of the two stems to remove (AF-7, Low). One source argues against deliberately opening the centre of the bush (C-1, unresolved; the majority view is recorded). Whether a gardener should wait when unsure which stem to remove was not addressed by any source (AF-8).

decision_notes.text: Remove the crossing or rubbing stem as ordinary dormant pruning.
Remove it completely, back to where it starts (the ground, the bud union, or the larger cane it grows from). Don't just shorten it.
If you need to choose which one, the few sources that give a rule say remove the weaker, thinner one and keep the stronger one.
Why: stems rubbing together damage each other's bark, which lets disease in.
Take care not to damage the stem you're keeping; cut a tangled stem out in sections rather than pulling it whole.

records.title: Inward-growing stems — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Far fewer sources than for crossing stems (IG AF-4, Low), because of thin coverage, not disagreement. Only one source states the full-removal cut for inward stems specifically (IG AF-5). One source argues against deliberately opening the centre (C-1, unresolved).

decision_notes.text: Remove a confirmed inward-growing stem the same way as a crossing stem. Few sources cover this, but none disagrees.
Remove it completely, back to where it starts. Don't just shorten it.

records.title: Damaged growth — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning, or the removal-only session of PKR-SGT-000001 v1.1 §2.1
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source defines "slight" versus "severe" precisely (AF-12). The answer is always to keep cutting down until healthy pith is found. The canker margin is worded "2–3 inches" or "well below" (AF-13). Disinfectant strength and how often to use it vary between sources (AF-15). Sources differ on how long to wait after frost damage (C-2).

decision_notes.text: Cut the damaged cane back until you reach healthy wood: white or pale-green pith. Brown, black or grey means keep cutting a little further down.
Slight damage: shorten just to healthy wood. Severe damage, or no living pith or buds below it: remove the whole cane at its base.
If it looks like canker or disease: cut well below the patch (commonly 2–3 inches, about 5–8 cm), clean your blades between cuts, and bin or burn the prunings.
If it looks like borer damage: cut below the damaged part until the pith is white or the hole is gone, then seal the fresh cut.

Frost or winter damage often doesn't show its full extent straight away. Sources advise waiting until live growth is emerging, so "Decide later" is the recommended choice for a frost-damaged cane. When you come back, I'll help you remove it even if the rose is growing.
Leave: sources advise cutting confirmed damage back to healthy wood.

records.title: Weak or congested growth — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The number of canes to keep varies by source and region, from 1–4 to 4–8 (C-2), so Pip gives a range. The sunscald caution comes from one source and applies to hot-summer climates (AF-18). The one-third caution comes from general (not rose-specific) advice about annual crown removal (AF-18). No source explains why weak canes should be removed before congestion is decided; the order follows how sources sequence the work (AF-14; U-6).

decision_notes.text: Weak cane: remove it completely, at its base or where it starts. Don't shorten it.
Crowded bush: remove whole canes, never part-shorten one. Keep the strongest, then aim for even spacing and an open, airy centre.
Keep roughly 3–7 strong canes, 4–6 typical, and fewer for a modest or young plant.
If the plant already looks weak or small, prune it lightly.
In hot-summer areas, leave some growth in the middle to shade the graft. Don't clear all the crowding at once.
Reaching inside the bush, wear eye protection and long-cuffed gloves.

records.title: The main framework — what to keep, what to remove, and how much to shorten

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Final heights vary widely between sources, so no fixed height is given (C1). How many canes to keep varies from 3 to 8 (C7). The one-third-per-year renewal figure comes from sources about shrub, landscape and climbing roses, not specifically Hybrid Teas or Floribundas (AF-20). The "replace a sickly bush" point is general shrub advice (AF-39).

decision_notes.text: Keep the strong, healthy canes spread around the base, aiming for an open centre.
Keep roughly 3–7 canes, 4–6 typical, and fewer for a modest or young plant.
Shorten kept canes by roughly a third to a half. Hybrid Teas are cut lower, or to fewer canes, than Floribundas. Grandifloras are pruned as Hybrid Teas.

doesnt_match_choices.label: Remove this old cane at its base

doesnt_match_notes.text: Remove old, grey, unproductive canes at their base, in favour of younger ones.
Renewing an old bush: remove about a third of the old canes each year, over several years, rather than all at once.
For a badly overgrown, weak or sickly bush, experienced local help is worth asking — such a bush is sometimes better replaced.

not_sure_choices.label: Keep it for now and reassess next pruning

records.title: Rootstock sucker — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: Established grafted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or provisional Grandiflora rose
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources disagree on tearing versus cutting at the origin, and no trial compares them on roses (C-1; R-4). Sources differ on removing early versus waiting for the first flowers to identify a sucker (C-5); Pip follows removal on confirmed origin. Each precaution rests on a single source (AF-22).

choices.label: Remove the sucker where it starts

decision_notes.text: Suckers draw strength from your rose and, left alone, can take it over.
Remove it early, while it's young — it's easier then.
Leave: sources advise removing confirmed suckers, because they weaken the rose.
If suckers keep coming back after removal, get experienced local help.

removal_method.text: Uncover the point where the sucker starts, clearing soil if needed, and remove it right there. Never cut it off at soil level — a sucker cut at the surface grows back.
Main method: with gloves on, grip the sucker as close to where it starts as you can and pull or tear it away. Tearing takes the hidden buds at its base with it, which makes regrowth less likely.
Alternative: some sources cut it cleanly, flush at the point where it starts. Sources disagree on which works better; both agree it must go at the origin.
Support the stem with one hand; afterwards refill the soil and firm it gently around the base.
Take care around the base when weeding or digging — root damage is linked with suckering.

records.title: Blind shoot — what to do once confirmed

common.applies_to: As PKR-OBS-000008
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources differ on where to cut (ARC-BUSHROSE-NOFLOWERS-01 C-4). The RHS cut point is used, per Founder decision D6(a).

choices.label: Cut it back to a strong bud

cut_method.text: Cut the blind shoot back by about half, to a strong bud. This should give a new shoot that can flower later in the season.
Other sources cut to the next leaf joint down, or to the next full five-leaflet leaf. Sources differ on where to cut.
One source removes a short blind shoot growing low on old wood completely.

records.title: Dead vs. living wood

common.applies_to: Established bush rose; dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: No Comparison Image PKR exists yet (documented gap, Founder decision 24 August 2026). Pith colour needs a cut and flexibility needs a bend, so neither can be judged from a photo.

content.look_for: Let's look for dead wood. Dead canes are usually brown, grey, black or shrivelled rather than green, and have no plump buds anywhere along them.

criteria.text: Bark colour: green suggests living; brown, grey, black or shrivelled suggests dead. Older or bronze canes can mislead.
Buds: plump visible buds suggest living; none anywhere suggests dead.
Sunken patches or lesions may be canker, not routine dead wood.
The surest check is the pith once cut: white or pale green is living; brown, grey or black is dead.
A living cane bends; a dead one is brittle and snaps.

content.photo_limit: A photo can't show the pith inside the cane or how it bends — check those on the plant.
content.confirm_question: Find that cane on your rose and look at it closely. Is it dead?
content.not_sure_guidance: Look again at the cane on the plant itself — its buds and its bark colour, right down low.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more dead canes?

records.title: Crossing or rubbing stems

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source describes what a rubbing wound looks like; the rubbing/crossing distinction below is an approved default, not a sourced finding. No beginner lookalike list exists (SC §6). Whether crossing and inward-growing stems usually occur together is unknown (SC §6).

content.look_for: Next, let's look for stems that cross each other or rub together.

criteria.text: A stem crossing another is a candidate. Crossing and rubbing are looked for together.
Bark damage, wear or a flattened face where two stems touch: treat as rubbing.
Stems close together with no contact or wear: treat as crossing, not rubbing.

content.photo_limit: One photo can't reliably show whether two stems actually touch. Look from several sides.
content.confirm_question: Follow both stems with your hands. Do they cross or touch?
content.not_sure_guidance: Take another photo from a different angle, and look again from another side.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more crossing or rubbing stems?

records.title: Inward-growing stems

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Most sources don't treat an inward-growing stem as its own defect; they prevent it by cutting to an outward-facing bud (IG AF-1, Moderate). Only a few name it as something to find and remove, and their standard is a soft judgement ("not growing in a graceful, natural direction"). A stem curving toward a gap in the light could be mistaken for inward growth. That's a plausible but unsourced caution, worth bearing in mind, not a rule (IG §6 default). No beginner lookalike list exists (IG §6).

content.look_for: Now let's look for stems growing into the centre of the bush.

criteria.text: A stem growing toward the centre of the bush is a candidate. No source gives a more specific sign.

content.photo_limit: One photo has real limits for judging which way a stem grows. Look from more than one side.
content.confirm_question: Check the stem on your rose from more than one side. Is it growing into the centre?
content.not_sure_guidance: Take another photo that shows the middle of the bush more clearly, and look again from another side.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more stems growing inward?

records.title: Damaged growth

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Causes aren't equally evidenced: sunscald rests on one source, and rodent and snow damage on one each (AF-2). No test exists for a split that isn't visible from outside (AF-6). Experts themselves disagree on whether canker can be diagnosed from a photo (C-3), so Pip always states its confidence. Sources are UK, US and Australian.

content.look_for: Now let's look for damaged growth — canes that are injured or diseased but not simply dead.

criteria.text: Canker: tan to purplish-brown sunken patches with cracking edges, tiny black dots, or dieback above a patch that rings the cane.
Frost or winter injury: browned or blackened tips and discoloured canes. Confirming it needs a cut into the pith.
Physical damage: a visibly broken cane, or worn, rubbed bark where canes touch.
Borer: a new tip that suddenly wilts, an entry hole, or slight swelling. A hole in the end of an old pruning cut is often a harmless wasp nest.
Not damage: mossy or spiny insect galls are generally harmless, and red, purple or yellow spots on young canes can be their normal colour.

content.photo_limit: A photo can show outside signs, but not what's happening inside the cane. If it's unclear, look closely at the plant rather than taking another photo.
content.confirm_question: Find that cane on your rose. Can you see damage like this?
content.not_sure_guidance: Look closely at that spot on the plant itself, not at a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more damaged stems?

records.title: Weak or congested growth

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: The two sources that put a number on "pencil thickness" disagree (about 6 mm versus 10 mm, C-1), so Pip uses no number. Why canes become weak is thinly evidenced; one source links congestion to weak growth, and one links old age to it (AF-2, Low). No source describes weak canes as arching or flopping, so that isn't used as a sign (U-2).

content.look_for: Let's look for weak canes — thinner than a pencil, twiggy or unproductive — and at whether the middle of the bush is crowded.

criteria.text: A cane thinner than about a pencil is a candidate weak cane. No number is used.
Twiggy or unproductive growth, with thin tips rather than full, lush canes.
Crowded: the bush is densely packed, especially at ground level, rather than open in the middle.
A thin cane with brown or reddish thorns may be this season's new growth rather than a weak cane.

content.photo_limit: Without a size reference, thickness can't be judged from a photo — hold a coin or pencil beside the cane. No photo can rule out crowding at the back of the bush.
content.confirm_question: Check the cane against a pencil, and look at the middle of the bush from more than one side. Is it weak, or is the bush crowded?
content.not_sure_guidance: Take a photo with a coin or pencil beside the cane, or look at the middle from another side, then check again.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more weak canes?

records.title: The main framework to retain

common.applies_to: Established bush rose (Hybrid Tea, Floribunda, provisional Grandiflora); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: Sources define "younger" differently (AF-9). No finding sets an age in years for "old" wood. The approved default treats canes older than about three years as candidates, which is a convention, not a measured fact (C6). No source describes how to spot new basal shoots on a dormant bush (AF-10).

content.look_for: Finally, let's choose the framework to keep: the strong canes spread around the base that will form the shape of your rose.

criteria.text: Keeper canes: strong, healthy, vigorous canes, generally the younger ones.
Target shape: an open centre, with kept canes spread evenly around the base, like a vase or the spokes of a wheel.
Old wood: grey, rough, scaly or crusty bark, sometimes with worn prickles.
New shoots from the base are a sign of good health and a way to renew the framework.
Keep your rose's own new canes from the base. First check where each starts: a shoot from below the bud union is a sucker.

content.photo_limit: A photo can show the outline, but not how vigorous a cane really is, the pith, or the base close up. Check those by hand.
content.confirm_question: Check this cane on your rose, down to the base. Is it a strong framework cane?
content.doesnt_match_label: No — it's old, grey or unproductive
content.not_sure_guidance: Look at the base close up and gently check the cane.
content.any_more_question: Are there any more canes to check?

records.title: Rootstock suckers — shoots from below the bud union

common.applies_to: Established grafted Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or provisional Grandiflora rose (passed PKR-SGT-000003). Any season (Founder decision D1(b)); PKR-SGT-000002 applies. Dormant session: point of origin only. Growing season: supporting signs may be added.
common.preserved_uncertainty: No source describes recognising a sucker on a dormant, leafless rose other than by where it starts (AF-10, Low). Sources disagree on how dependable leaf clues are (C-2), and rootstocks differ by country (AF-9; New Zealand mainly uses *Rosa multiflora* or strains of it), so Pip gives no rootstock-specific cues (R-3 default). One source says a rootstock stub left above the union can also sucker (AF-14, Low; C-6); this isn't used to classify shoots. No source gives a prickle or cane rule (AF-8). No source says what a photo can establish (R-2). Sources are UK, US, Australian and New Zealand.

content.look_for: Let's check for suckers. A sucker is a shoot from the rootstock your rose was grafted onto, below the bud union — the knobbly join near the base. It isn't your rose's own new cane.

criteria.text: Where the shoot starts is the deciding check: below the bud union is a sucker; at the union or just above it is your rose's own new cane, which you keep.
A sucker can start below the soil, sometimes a little away from the plant.
Planting depth varies, so the bud union may be above, at or below the soil.

content.photo_limit: A photo can't show where a shoot starts, especially under the soil. I never decide a shoot is a sucker from a photo.
content.confirm_question: Follow the shoot down with your fingers. Does it start below the bud union, or at or above it?
content.doesnt_match_label: At or above the bud union
content.doesnt_match_note: That's your rose's own new cane. Keep it — the rose's own basal canes are valuable. It's considered in the framework step.
content.not_sure_guidance: That's alright. It's easy to confuse these, even for experienced gardeners. Look again at where the shoot starts, on the plant, not in a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more shoots like this coming from the base?

sucker_steps.hasShoot: Is there a shoot coming from the base of your rose, or from the ground near it?
sucker_steps.unionVisible: Can you see the bud union — the knobbly join near the base where your rose was grafted?
sucker_steps.noUnion: Then I won't call it a sucker. The union may just be buried. If you like, gently clear a little soil and look again — otherwise leave the shoot, and ask experienced local help if you're concerned.
sucker_steps.ownRoot: If you know your rose grows on its own roots (it wasn't grafted), shoots from the base are the same rose, so none is a sucker — keep them.
sucker_steps.supporting: In the growing season only, these can help you look, but never decide on their own: sucker leaves are often paler or smaller or have a different number of leaflets (though the "seven leaflets" rule isn't reliable); sucker flowers differ from your rose's; suckers are often unusually vigorous, straight and tall.

records.title: Blind shoots — healthy shoots with no flower bud at the tip

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora rose (passed PKR-SGT-000003), in the growing season
common.preserved_uncertainty: The cause of blind shoots is not known (ARC-BUSHROSE-NOFLOWERS-01 AF-22, C-3). No source says what a photograph can show. No source says how soon a shoot without a bud counts as blind; Pip offers this check only once other shoots have buds or flowers (approved default, Decision 2).

content.look_for: Let's check for blind shoots. A blind shoot grows and leafs normally, but has no flower bud at its tip.

criteria.text: The shoot and its leaves can look perfectly healthy; what's missing is a flower bud at the tip.
The tip may look empty, or dried up.
Nobody knows for certain what causes blind shoots.

content.photo_limit: I can't confirm a blind shoot from a photo. Look at the tip of the shoot itself.
content.confirm_question: Look closely at the very tip of the shoot. Is there a flower bud there?
content.doesnt_match_note: Then it isn't a blind shoot. Leave it to flower.
content.not_sure_guidance: That's alright. Look again at the tip on the plant, not in a photo.
content.any_more_question: Can you see any more shoots like this, with leaves but no bud at the tip?

offer_when.question: Do other shoots on your rose already have flower buds or flowers?
offer_when.not_yet_note: Then it's too early to call a shoot blind. Come back to this check once other shoots on your rose have buds or flowers.

records.title: Dormancy gate — is the rose in the window for structural pruning?

common.applies_to: Established bush rose. Prerequisite for structural and whole-bush pruning (PKR-OBS/DEC-000002, 000003, 000005, 000006, and any shortening or shaping of healthy canes). Does not govern removal of wood confirmed dead, damaged or diseased (PKR-DEC-000001, PKR-DEC-000004), which follows the removal-only session.
common.preserved_uncertainty: AF-3 (Moderate): in mild or warm-winter climates, full leaf loss may not occur and premature bud break is a documented risk — the gardener should judge dormancy by bud state specifically, not by whether leaves are present. A follow-up commission (FRD-BUSHROSE-DORMANCY-02, submitted alongside this package) is testing whether the bud-swell signal itself needs a stated mild-climate exception; this gate's wording will be revised if that research changes the picture.

content.question: Look closely at the dormant buds along your rose's canes. Has active new growth already begun — buds swelling, breaking open, or new leaves emerging anywhere on the plant — or does the plant still appear dormant?
content.caveat: If your climate is mild or unusually warm, judge this by bud state specifically — not by whether the leaves have dropped. In milder climates a rose doesn't always lose all its leaves, and buds can sometimes break earlier than expected.

answers.dormant: Still dormant — buds are tight and closed, or just beginning to swell; no new leaves have opened anywhere
answers.growing: Active new growth is already well underway — leaves have opened and new shoots are clearly growing

content.notSureFallback: That's alright — have another look at the buds specifically, not the leaves: are they still tight and closed, or have any started to swell or open? If you're still not certain after a closer look, the safest choice is to treat the rose as not quite ready yet, and check back in a week or two.

intro.text: Your rose is already growing, so this is not the time for full pruning. Pruning hard now can cost you flowers. But you can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased.

removalOnly.notSureIntro: Since we can't be sure your rose is still dormant, we'll leave full pruning for now — check back in a week or two. You can still remove wood that is dead, damaged or diseased today.

conditions.text: Remove only the wood you've confirmed. Don't shorten or shape healthy canes today.
Go gently and avoid damaging the new leaves and shoots.
Cut back until the pith is white or pale green, exactly as at any other time.
For anything that looks like canker or disease, the usual care applies: cut well below the affected part, clean your blades, and bin the prunings.

lateSeason.text: Late in the season (advice only): sources advise against pruning late in the growing season, because it can encourage new growth that winter cold may damage. Diseased wood is the exception — remove it whenever you find it. Sources don't say whether dead (as distinct from diseased) wood is exempt.

records.title: Recently planted gate — is the rose established enough for full pruning guidance?

common.applies_to: Established or recently planted bush rose; prerequisite check, before the five non-dead-wood pruning observations proceed. Does not restrict dead-wood removal (see §4).
common.preserved_uncertainty: AF-1 (Moderate): the ~3-year threshold is an approximate range from the strongest available source, not a precise, validated figure; RHS's shorter "first winter" guidance remains unreconciled (ARC §5). AF-2 (Low): the fallback signals are unvalidated in combination and may not apply equally across own-root and grafted roses.

content.question: Do you know approximately when this rose was planted? If so, has it been growing in this spot for about three years or more?

answers.recent: No, it's more recent than that

content.fallback_intro: That's alright — plenty of gardeners aren't sure. Let's check three signs together.

fallback_questions.label: Is it putting out active new growth right now?
Does it have noticeably more canes than a newly bought rose (more than about 3)?
Does the base feel firmly rooted when you gently test it?

content.restricted_reason_recent: This rose hasn't been in the ground long enough yet for the full check, so we'll only look at dead wood today.
content.restricted_reason_fallback: We can't confirm this rose is established enough yet, so we'll only look at dead wood today, to stay safe.

records.title: Rose-type gate — is this rose a supported bush-rose type?

common.applies_to: Any rose a gardener brings to the pruning journey. This prerequisite check runs before every other gate and every observation, dead wood included.
common.preserved_uncertainty: (1) Pip can't tell a rose's type from photos or a dormant plant (AF-20, R-1). The gate relies entirely on what the gardener has been told. (2) Some cultivars are classed differently by different authorities (ARC §4, AF-5), so a stated type isn't infallible. (3) Grandiflora is included provisionally only. It's largely absent from NZ classification sources (AF-4), and Pip gives no Grandiflora-specific pruning guidance (R-4).

content.question: Do you know what type of rose this is — from its label or pot tag, a receipt or nursery listing, or someone experienced who has told you?

answers.label: Another type (shrub, English, patio, miniature, groundcover, climbing or rambling, standard, old garden or species rose)
The label only says "bush rose" or "rose bush"
I know its variety name but not its type

content.grandifloraNote: Grandiflora is supported provisionally. It gets the same guidance as a Hybrid Tea; there is no Grandiflora-specific advice.

roseFinder.text: The New Zealand Rose Society's Rose Finder lists a type for each rose it holds. Look the name up there, then answer this question again. If you can't find it, the answer is the same as "I don't know".

journalOnly.base: I can't yet help prune this rose. My pruning guidance so far covers only Hybrid Tea, Floribunda and Grandiflora bush roses.
journalOnly.excluded: That type isn't one my pruning guidance covers yet.
journalOnly.bushOnly: "Bush" on a label doesn't say which type a rose is — garden retailers use it for patio, shrub and groundcover roses too.
journalOnly.unknown: Without a confirmed type I can't be sure the guidance fits, and I don't try to identify roses from photos, because that's unreliable even for experts.
journalOnly.keep: Your rose stays in your garden list as a journal: photos, notes and history all remain available. If you later confirm it is a Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora, you can answer this question again.
journalOnly.help: If you want the type identified, a local rose society or an experienced rose grower is the best place to ask.

journalOnly.help: If you want the type identified, a local rose society or an experienced rose grower is the best place to ask.
